newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: New offers at WTO telecoms talks encouraging.
newsitem.headline: New offers at WTO telecoms talks encouraging.

text.p: Ten countries submitted new or revised offers on Friday for a global pact on liberalising telecommunications markets which faces a February 15 deadline, the chairman said.

This brought to 54 the number of countries which have filed offers, with 14 new or revised offers expected next week, according to Neil McMillan, the British official who chairs the negotiating group of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
"We've actually had not a bad harvest of new offers," McMillan told a news briefing after the one-day, closed talks. "Overall, I can say we are very encouraged..."
The telecommunications negotiations, part of the leftover business from the Uruguay Round which ended in December 1993, aim to break down barriers in the $600 billion world market.
The talks failed to meet a deadline of last April after the United States said offers from emerging economies were not good enough for it to open its domestic market to foreign operators.

The European Union also provided technical details on its offer of last November making clear that it covers transport of any signals -- including of sound, data or image -- but not the content or separate commercial activity, trade sources said.
EU negotiators said that the long-running WTO talks were "on track" for a successful conclusion in two weeks.
"We're very happy with the revised and new offers this week," an EU negotiator told Reuters in Geneva.
"Things seem to be on track for a successful conclusion."
The United States had also indicated in the closed-door meeting that it was encouraged and said it "looked forward" to the successful wrap-up of the talks, according to trade sources.
"The United States said it was confident of the positive continuation of new and improved offers," said one.
No U.S. trade envoy in Geneva could be reached for comment.

Referring to the U.S. Deputy Trade Representative, one trade source said: "Clearly in the end anybody who is engaged in this negotiation, and that obviously includes Jeff Lang, is going to have to make a a decision about whether what he has got in his hands is sellable to the interests that he represents.
"That applies to any delegation. But the Americans are extremely important in this negotiation."
Bulgaria, El Salvador, Indonesia, Romania and South Africa submitted new offers, while Australia, Czech Republic, Mexico, Poland and Singapore presented revised offers, McMillan said.
"That brings us up to submitted offers from 54 governments. So we're not going too badly there at all," he added.
"We've had new undertakings from people, most of whom said they would be providing these offers by early next week, some perhaps slightly later," he added.
These included Bangladesh and Malaysia -- the latter a key hold-out which had not actually taken part at all before.
Countries pledging to submit revised offers next week were Japan, Israel, New Zealand, Peru, Pakistan and Thailand.
A further six new offers were expected, including from Barbados, Jamaica, Ghana and Egypt. Eight revised offers were expected next week -- including South Korea and India.
The United States has made clear it sees participation of Indonesia and Malaysia, both "tiger economies", as vital to create the "critical mass" it says is needed for the pact.
Washington's stance is key as it pulled out of the earlier talks saying not enough countries were involved for it to open its market to all, as would be required under WTO rules.
The WTO negotiating group will meet again on Monday, February 10 and high-level officials have been invited.
"The discussion of offers is really taking place now between the delegations bilaterally," a trade source said.
